articles.text: City staff submitted a revised Housing Element to the California Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD) on May 9, and comments from the state were due yesterday, May 23. The City Council voted to adopt the Element on March 20. However, the Element is not yet state-compliant. This drafting cycle is repeated every eight years. The revised Element, with tracked changes, is available at bit.ly/43aXR8x. Scouts from Piedmont Troop 6 will present the colors. The program will include the traditional placing of a wreath and a 21-gun salute to honor those who have died serving our country. Members of the TOSCA singing group, the Piedmont Highlanders Pipe & Drum Trio, and the Dave Hartman Trio will participate in a musical salute to the fallen. Guest speakers will be announced. Following the program, docent Dennis Evanosky will offer a tour of the cemetery’s Grand Army of the Republic plot. articles.text: Piedmont Fire Chief As summer nears, many of our thoughts turn to barbecues, vacations, and days at the beach. As Piedmont’s Fire Chief, my mind goes to a thornier subject – the approach of fire season, a threat that looms larger each year as wildfires across California become more frequent and severe. The urban forest that makes Piedmont so beautiful also brings vulnerability. The lush greenery brought on by heavy rains this winter will soon turn to thick, dry vegetation. While it’s not possible to extinguish wildfire risk entirely, we can all sprinkle a dose of protection on our community by taking a few simple steps – starting in our own back (and front) yards. I’m talking about vegetation management. Probably not the most glamorous task on your summertime to-do list, but one of the most important. Don’t “leaf” your most significant investment to chance – a well-prepared yard acts as a buffer zone, providing a layer of defense to your home in the event of a wildfire. The first step in weeding out risk is to clear your yard of debris and flammable materials. Do you have leaves, pine needles on the ground or in your gutter? Get rid of them. Dead plants hiding on the property? They need to go. Using the space under your deck to store extra paint or propane containers? Move them elsewhere. Next, you want to create space between plants, structures, and other objects. Trim your vulnerability by removing any branches that hang over your roof or near a chimney. Move patio furniture and wood piles away from vegetation. Prune trees so the lowest branches are at least six feet from the ground, or three times the height of shrubs below. By removing fuel sources that could act as a “ladder,” you make it harder for a fire to move from the ground to the treetops. Finally, keep all vegetation in your yard in good health. People often ask whether a specific type of tree or shrub is safe to plant. Native plants have evolved to adapt to fire conditions in California. But even non-natives, if well maintained and watered, can be fire resistive. Whatever landscaping you’ve chosen, you can stem fire risk by trimming away dead or dying material, including removing shedding bark and leaves from Eucalyptus trees, which are especially flammable. It’s best to not have plants within five feet of your home, but if you do, take extra care to keep them well watered. Taking these simple, but essential steps to prepare your yard at the beginning of every summer will create the peace of mind that comes with knowing you’ve done what you can to protect your property. Even better, your actions will serve as a model for others. The steps we take as individuals have the potential to ignite a ripple effect, spreading awareness and inspiring our neighbors to prepare their own yards. When each of us plants the seeds of safety on our own property, we cultivate a collective defense, increasing the likelihood of slowing or containing spread of a wildfire. Find helpful tools, including a printable yard-maintenance checklist and links to other useful resources on our website at piedmont.ca.gov/vegetation. And remember, your Fire Department is here to help. If you have questions or would like us to come inspect your yard, call us at 420- 3030. Let’s blaze a safer path together. “Dude...do you have an attitude problem?”

articles.text: PG&E workers returned to the Piedmont Community Pool site on Saturday, May 20 to complete disconnecting power from the former Carriage House and pool locker room, work that began in February. With gas and electrical lines fully removed, contractors can continue to excavate without further delays. The one-day job, which PG&E workers were scheduled to perform the week of May 8, involved the pulling of an electrical line which used to service the now-demolished Carriage House on Magnolia Avenue. Although demolition-related utility work is done, Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales said that PG&E “will need to return to provide electrical power to the new pool [facilities] later in the project.” Meanwhile, contractors continue to excavate and trucks continue to haul away soil. An estimated five more weeks of truck activity is expected. The soil is being hauled to different sites depending on whether or not the soil is contaminated. Gonzales explained: “The soil near the [former] Carriage House particularly has diesel fuel in it due to vehicle runoff and old wood preservative sprays, so it’s going to a waste management landfill in Livermore called Altamont. Cleaner soil on the site is being hauled off for what’s called ‘beneficial reuse,’ to be used as cover in future construction projects elsewhere.” A subcontractor, GEOCON, is testing the soil for chemical pollutants and Coastland Civil Engineering is tracking this excavation and testing process to make sure that it conforms to state environmental and building codes. For more information, visit piedmont.ca.gov/newpool. Those with questions about the project may contact Construction Manager George Sanen of Griffin Structures by email at gsanen@ griffinstructures.com. Photo courtesy of Public Works Dept. articles.text: Piedmont Police were notified by the Oakland Police Department on Tuesday, May 23 that a crew of nine juveniles ranging in age from 12-17 were arrested on May 21. OPD has connected the group to 35 reported robberies in the East Bay. The locations are 14 neighborhoods in Oakland, including Rockridge, Grand Lake, Mosswood, and Temescal, as well as El Cerrito and Piedmont. “In recent weeks, the City of Oakland has been terrorized by violent individuals wreaking havoc and committing robberies upon unassuming community members. The Oakland Police Department (OPD) is investigating several different robbery series citywide, where robbery crews are brazenly victimizing individuals at alarming rates,” a press release from OPD states. Piedmont Police do not yet know if any of the suspects are connected with the mugging and assault of two Piedmont women in their 70s on May 6. The arrest of the nine juvenile suspects occurred when Oakland officers spotted a vehicle wanted in connection with a series of robberies and tracked the vehicle to the 100 block of 14th Street on the westside of Lake Merritt. As officers arrived, multiple occupants exited the vehicle and went into a nearby establishment; the vehicle took off at high speed. An Oakland PD helicopter tracked the vehicle to the area of 6th Avenue and East 15th Street. Four occupants got out of the vehicle and fled on foot. Officers followed the juveniles on foot and quickly detained them. Additionally, five individuals were safely taken into custody at the establishment by Lake Merritt. The investigation is ongoing. Anyone with additional information is asked to contact the Oakland Police Department Robbery Section at 238-3326. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. pages.text: Wednesday, May 24, 2023 3 Pool update PG&E delays over, soil removal continues By Selen Ozturk PG&E workers returned to the Piedmont Community Pool site on Saturday, May 20 to complete disconnecting power from the former Carriage House and pool locker room, work that began in February. With gas and electrical lines fully removed, contractors can continue to excavate without further delays. The one-day job, which PG&E workers were scheduled to perform the week of May 8, involved the pulling of an electrical line which used to service the now-demolished Carriage House on Magnolia Avenue. Although demolition-related utility work is done, Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales said that PG&E “will need to return to provide electrical power to the new pool [facilities] later in the project.” Meanwhile, contractors continue to excavate and trucks continue to haul away soil. An estimated five more weeks of truck activity is expected. The soil is being hauled to different sites depending on whether or not the soil is contaminated. Gonzales explained: “The soil near the [former] Carriage House particularly has diesel fuel in it due to vehicle runoff and old wood preservative sprays, so it’s going to a waste management landfill in Livermore called Altamont. Cleaner soil on the site is being hauled off for what’s called ‘beneficial reuse,’ to be used as cover in future construction projects elsewhere.” A subcontractor, GEOCON, is testing the soil for chemical pollutants and Coastland Civil Engineering is tracking this excavation and testing process to make sure that it conforms to state environmental and building codes. For more information, visit piedmont.ca.gov/newpool. Those with questions about the project may contact Construction Manager George Sanen of Griffin Structures by email at gsanen@ griffinstructures.com. Photo courtesy of Public Works Dept. Piedmont Community Pool contractors on Magnolia Avenue load soil into a truck to be hauled away. Oakland Police arrest 9 juveniles connected to 35 robberies By Jay Russell Piedmont Police were notified by the Oakland Police Department on Tuesday, May 23 that a crew of nine juveniles ranging in age from 12-17 were arrested on May 21. OPD has connected the group to 35 reported robberies in the East Bay. The locations are 14 neighborhoods in Oakland, including Rockridge, Grand Lake, Mosswood, and Temescal, as well as El Cerrito and Piedmont. “In recent weeks, the City of Oakland has been terrorized by violent individuals wreaking havoc and committing robberies upon unassuming community members. The Oakland Police Department (OPD) is investigating several different robbery series citywide, where robbery crews are brazenly victimizing individuals at alarming rates,” a press release from OPD states. Piedmont Police do not yet know if any of the suspects are connected with the mugging and assault of two Piedmont women in their 70s on May 6. The arrest of the nine juvenile suspects occurred when Oakland officers spotted a vehicle wanted in connection with a series of robberies and tracked the vehicle to the 100 block of 14th Street on the westside of Lake Merritt. As officers arrived, multiple occupants exited the vehicle and went into a nearby establishment; the vehicle took off at high speed. An Oakland PD helicopter tracked the vehicle to the area of 6th Avenue and East 15th Street. Four occupants got out of the vehicle and fled on foot. Officers followed the juveniles on foot and quickly detained them. Additionally, five individuals were safely taken into custody at the establishment by Lake Merritt. The investigation is ongoing. As Piedmont’s Fire Chief, my mind goes to a thornier subject – the approach of fire season, a threat that looms larger each year as wildfires across California become more frequent and severe. The urban forest that makes Piedmont so beautiful also brings vulnerability. The lush greenery brought on by heavy rains this winter will soon turn to thick, dry vegetation. While it’s not possible to extinguish wildfire risk entirely, we can all sprinkle a dose of protection on our community by taking a few simple steps – starting in our own back (and front) yards. I’m talking about vegetation management. Probably not the most glamorous task on your summertime to-do list, but one of the most important. Don’t “leaf” your most significant investment to chance – a well-prepared yard acts as a buffer zone, providing a layer of defense to your home in the event of a wildfire. The first step in weeding out risk is to clear your yard of debris and flammable materials. Do you have leaves, pine needles on the ground or in your gutter? Get rid of them. Dead plants hiding on the property? They need to go. Using the space under your deck to store extra paint or propane containers? Move them elsewhere. Next, you want to create space between plants, structures, and other objects. Trim your vulnerability by removing any branches that hang over your roof or near a chimney. Move patio furniture and wood piles away from vegetation. Prune trees so the lowest branches are at least six feet from the ground, or three times the height of shrubs below. By removing fuel sources that could act as a “ladder,” you make it harder for a fire to move from the ground to the treetops. Finally, keep all vegetation in your yard in good health. People often ask whether a specific type of tree or shrub is safe to plant. Native plants have evolved to adapt to fire conditions in California. But even non-natives, if well maintained and watered, can be fire resistive. Whatever landscaping you’ve chosen, you can stem fire risk by trimming away dead or dying material, including removing shedding bark and leaves from Eucalyptus trees, which are especially flammable. It’s best to not have plants within five feet of your home, but if you do, take extra care to keep them well watered. Taking these simple, but essential steps to prepare your yard at the beginning of every summer will create the peace of mind that comes with knowing you’ve done what you can to protect your property. Even better, your actions will serve as a model for others. The steps we take as individuals have the potential to ignite a ripple effect, spreading awareness and inspiring our neighbors to prepare their own yards. When each of us plants the seeds of safety on our own property, we cultivate a collective defense, increasing the likelihood of slowing or containing spread of a wildfire. Find helpful tools, including a printable yard-maintenance checklist and links to other useful resources on our website at piedmont.ca.gov/vegetation. And remember, your Fire Department is here to help. If you have questions or would like us to come inspect your yard, call us at 420- 3030. Let’s blaze a safer path together. articles.text: Members of the League of Women Voters of Piedmont (LWVP) attended the biennial California League of Women Voters Convention this past weekend in San Francisco May 19 to 21. The convention drew over 200 delegates, staff, and League members from across the state. In attendance as delegates from Piedmont were Jennifer Trainor, Lois Corrin, Lorrel Plimier, and Kathleen Quenneville. Plimier, the president of LWVP, was voted in as a member of the Board of Directors for California. In addition to taking care of required League business, the Convention featured speakers and panels on voting and voting rights who drew attention to barriers to voting, what motivates people to vote, and what sources of information voters rely on. Friday and Saturday were full of workshops and caucuses on topics including Homelessness and Affordable Housing, California Water, Community Outreach, Social Justice, and Creating a Culture of Belonging. Trainor and Plimier led the workshop on Community Outreach, which included panelists from the electoral alliance San Francisco Rising, the college student nonprofit CALPIRG Students, and the Council on American-Islamic Relations. A highlight of this year’s Convention was the Drag for Democracy fundraiser on Saturday evening that not only entertained attendees with local drag celebrities, but also gave awards to several local politicians and activists who work for LGBTQ+ people, rights, and equality. articles.text: On Thursday, May 19, the Piedmont School District Wellness Center unveiled its new counseling room in Piedmont Middle School. Dozens of students made their way to the event during their lunch break to check out the new space and learn about Wellness Center offerings. The staff greeted students with a table of healthy snacks and giveaways. The Wellness Center provides counseling services, mental health support, and education to Piedmont High School, Middle School and Millennium students. During the 2022-2023 school year, the Wellness Center logged over 2,000 visits by students at the three schools. The new space at PMS was furnished and decorated thanks to a parent-run Wellness Center Support Committee and funded by community donations. Wellness Center staff will use the space to continue offering counseling by appointment during school hours and drop-in support during lunch breaks. Piedmont’s middle and high schools are very fortunate to have the level of support the Wellness Center offers students. “Our program here is unique,” said PHS Assistant Principal Irma Muñoz, who oversees the Wellness Center. “Not all schools can offer students this depth of mental health support.” Dr. Sari Sanghvi, who co-supervises the Wellness Center with Dr. Alisa Crovetti, said, “It is our priority to put mental health at the forefront, as well as to take a preventative and proactive approach to supporting the mental health of our students.” In a recent survey by the district, parents ranked student mental health as a top priority, second only to academic curriculum. With funding from the district, Alameda County and community donations, the Wellness Center 7th grade students Ethan Block, Quinton Cole, Lukas Toth and Miles Simon show their support for the new Wellness Center counseling room at Piedmont Middle School. Wellness Center and its PMS staff: Dr. Nicholas Saldivar, Counselor Charles Garrett, Dr. Alisa Crovetti, Dr. Sari Sanghvi, PHS Assistant Principal Irma Muñoz, and counselors Linnéa Limón and Lizzie Pfeiffer. 7th graders Olivia Stevens and Hannah Joerger check out the new Wellness Center space. provides two supervisors and seven interns who offer counseling services. The Wellness Center also provides weekly opportunities throughout the school year for the Center’s therapists in training to learn from experts in the field on various topics that are directly applicable to supporting students. Past topics have included solution-focused therapy, suicide and substance abuse prevention, and how to support gender-expansive students. Earlier this month, the Wellness Center obtained American Psychological Association (APA) accreditation, a highly prestigious recognition that involves a rigorous, two-year evaluation process. PUSD’s Wellness Center is also a member of the U.C. Berkeley Psychology Internship Consortium (BPIC). “With our recent APA accreditation and BPIC affiliation, we have access to the highest caliber of predoctoral psychology graduate students to continue providing high-level service to Piedmont students,” said Crovetti. To connect with someone at the Wellness Center or if interested in joining the Wellness Center Support Committee, call Wellness Center Health Clerk Viki Salazar at 594-2803, or e-mail vsalazar@piedmont.k12. ca.us.

articles.text: Young People’s Symphony Orchestra, the oldest youth orchestra in California and the oldest independent youth orchestra in the nation, is now accepting new members. Auditions are being conducted for trumpet, trombone, bass trombone, tuba, bassoon, oboe, violin, viola, and double bass. Founded in 1936 in Berkeley, YPSO has been led by conductor and Music Director David Ramadanoff for 35 years, with an orchestra of more than 100 musicians from schools through the greater Bay Area. YPSO will tour and perform in Japan next year, and will perform in the Bay Area Youth Orchestra Festival at Davies Symphony Hall in San Francisco. Submission of screening videos are due by June 1. For details and registration: www.ypsomusic.org/how-to-join YPSO rehearses most Monday evenings at First Congregational Church of Oakland, 2501 Harrison Street from 6:00-9:30 p.m. There is also an annual weekend retreat in the Fall in Carmel Valley and several Saturday afternoon intensives during the year.

articles.text: I am an ADHD Focus Coach in Piedmont working with students and people with Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, helping them overcome obstacles and achieve their goals. I am certified in Applied Positive Psychology and use my education and my personal experience with ADHD to coach my clients. This week I am talking about different types of mindfulness besides meditation that people with ADHD can implement to improve their lives. Mindfulness is “a mental state achieved by focusing one’s awareness on the present moment.” This can be particularly difficult for people with ADHD who are often easily distracted. The most well-known method of mindfulness is mindfulness meditation which is where you cultivate more mindfulness through a dedicated meditation practice. This can be very beneficial for people with ADHD and I recommend it to clients with great success. With that being said, not everyone with ADHD has the desire to or the ability to develop a consistent meditation practice especially children with ADHD. I am going to discuss a few ways to be mindful without a meditation practice. The first practice I recommend to my clients is mindful eating. This is a practice where you put away the screens and anything else you might have to distract you for the time that you’re eating. This can help you savor the food more and enjoy the present moment while still having a sensation to focus on. To give this a try, sit down with your favorite meal and enjoy the tastes and smells with less distractions. The second practice I recommend is a sensory check in. This can also be a grounding exercise for people with anxiety. To give this a try, you’re going to want to identify in your mind one thing you can taste, one thing you can touch, one thing you can smell, one thing you can hear and one thing you can see. This is another way to bring yourself back into the present moment and feel a little bit more grounded there. There are lots of ways to experience the present moment without a dedicated meditation practice. These 1are just a few that I’ve seen success with my clients. With ADHD, it can often be difficult to sit for an entire meditation practice but practicing mindfulness can help with ADHD symptoms over time and has benefits for everyone. articles.text: Members of Wildwood Dads Club and friends woke up with the sun to hit the links on Friday, May 12, for an all-day golf tournament. The event, in its inaugural year, began with a party bus from Piedmont to Oakmoore Golf Course in Stockton. After a successful year of fundraising for the school, the Dads Club put together the trip as another bonding experience. The off the beaten path location in Stockton was chosen because the entire course is designed to be rented out for small tournaments. Dads Club President Adam Fishman served as the “Drink Cart Guy.” Instead of a companion golfer next to him he teamed up with an industrial Mike Niver (left), Reed Johnson, Paul Kennedy and Greg Wheeler Wildwood Dads Club golfers ready to play at Oakmoore Golf Course sized cooler. Fishman patrolled the course serving drinks to parched golfers on a day with the temperature in the 90s. He also provided them with veggie burritos and chips. The day’s competition was a shotgun start with four groups of four in a best-ball tournament. Trophies were awarded for long drive on hole 18 (Mike Stearns), best golf outfit (Jay Russell), longest putt (Matt Derrigo), and best team (Max Roman’s foursome). “Wildwood dads convened for a day of teambuilding and camaraderie. The event culminated a successful school year of volunteerism and fundraising for Wildwood Elementary School,” confirmed dad Scott Zengel. The golfing ended in the early afternoon just as the Stockton heat kicked into high gear. Wildwood Dads and friends proceeded to fire up the barbeque for spareribs and hot dogs as they shared the day’s bloopers, high notes, and adventures. The success of the first tournament is likely to make it an annual tradition. articles.text: Piedmont freshman Lucas Smolko capped off a tremendous debut season on the varsity tennis team by advancing to the finals of the Division 2 North Coast Section Individual Tournament on Tuesday, May 16 at McKinleyville High School in Northern California.. Smolko lost in the finals to freshman Gus Grumet from University High in San Francisco, 6-3, 6-1. It sets up three more years of top-level tennis by both players. “It was really an awesome experience. I wasn’t sure if I was going to get into the tournament when I first started WACC, so I was just happy to get in. I didn’t have any high expectations. I had a lot of fun and got a great result… Gus is a really good player all-around, I knew he was tough going in. Almost any time I hit to his backhand, he gained a point,” said Smolko. Grumet is one of the topranked freshmen in the U.S. “Lucas was seeded second and was able to live up to his seed,” said Piedmont assistant coach Corey Reich. “The No. 1 seed, Gus Grumet, is ranked No. 5 in the U.S. in his age category. The first set was the best tennis I’ve seen Lucas play. He was bombing first serves at a high percentage, ripping forehands and backhands, and keeping Gus as off balance as possible. The Highlanders competed in nine events and were able to qualify in two for the 2023 CIF State Championship in Clovis by way of top-three finishes. Senior Parker Long wound up winning the 800 meter run with a blistering time of 1:53.80, coming just .55 of a second away from matching his record time. He came in .80 of a second ahead of Joaquin Foster of San Domenico and a field of 12 finalists. “I watched all of the runners in the prelims and I got the sense going in that people were going to go out fast at the start and everyone would be aggressive. My strategy was to let that happen, stay in the mix, but not make a big move until late in the race… When people go out faster, that means they’ll have less of a kick at the end of the race. articles.text: Photo courtesy of MyScorebookLive.com Piedmont High will introduce Girls’ Flag Football as an official school sport in the fall of 2023. It’s an exciting time for Piedmont High girls’ athletes. In the fall, PHS will introduce girls’ flag football as an official sport, and will compete with eight other schools in the Western Alameda County Conference, The Highlanders are expected to field both Varsity and Junior Varsity rosters. “It looks like we’ll have a varsity and JV team,” said PHS Athletic Director Bradley Smet. “There’s a lot of girls interested and I’m getting questions about it every day. We’ll have athletes from other sports who have been recruiting friends.” The varsity roster will be coached by Piedmont High English teacher Beth Black, with Hayley Adams as manager of the JV team. “We’ve had just one interest meeting and there were girls in that room who were so excited. The intensity about being able to play football was exhilarating. Not one of them has played the game. I’m very excited about the prospect of building this from the ground up,” said Black. “It’s the first-ever flag football team is coming here. This is a nation-wide endeavor. I’m hoping the Rec. Department can start a feeder program for middle school athletes,” added Black. Piedmont will play teams from Alameda, Berkeley, Encinal, Hayward, Mt. Eden, San Leandro, and Tennyson in the WACC and have a season-ending league tournament similar to water polo. The Highlanders will practice and play their games on the outfield of Humphries Diamond. Per league standards, the field of play can range between 50-80 yards in length and 30-50 yards in width, including a 10-yard end zone. “We’ll likely have over 20 games. There will be a league tournament at the end of the season.” Games are played in a 7-on-7 format with all seven players eligible as pass receivers, including the center after snapping the ball. There are no punts, field goals, or extra-point attempts—touchdowns are worth six points, while you can gain one extra point by converting a 5-yard play or twopoints from 10-yards. Punts automatically place the ball deep in the opponent’s half of the field. It’s a fast-paced game with two 22-minute halves, including a running clock for the first 20-minutes of each half. Quarterbacks are only allowed to scramble once every four downs, while defenses are allowed one pass rusher. Defense’s sending two pass rushers enables the quarterback to scramble past the line of scrimmage regardless of whether they’ve already used their running ability within the four downs. It’s not just a passing league as well with handoffs also permitted on offense. “The quarterback can run but only per every series of downs, so we’ll going to be working with that on how we’re going to structure our offense with handoffs to a running back, or even a handoff to our quarterback,” said Black. By Jonathan Comeaux It’s an exciting time for Piedmont High girls’ athletes. In the fall, PHS will introduce girls’ flag football as an official sport, and will compete with eight other schools in the Western Alameda County Conference, The Highlanders are expected to field both Varsity and Junior Varsity rosters. “It looks like we’ll have a varsity and JV team,” said PHS Athletic Director Bradley Smet. “There’s a lot of girls interested and I’m getting questions about it every day. We’ll have athletes from other sports who have been recruiting friends.” The varsity roster will be coached by Piedmont High English teacher Beth Black, with Hayley Adams as manager of the JV team. “We’ve had just one interest meeting and there were girls in that room who were so excited. The intensity about being able to play football was exhilarating. Not one of them has played the game. I’m very excited about the prospect of building this from the ground up,” said Black. “It’s the first-ever flag football team is coming here. This is a nation-wide endeavor. I’m hoping the Rec. Department can start a feeder program for middle school athletes,” added Black. Piedmont will play teams from Alameda, Berkeley, Encinal, Hayward, Mt. Eden, San Leandro, and Tennyson in the WACC and have a season-ending league tournament similar to water polo. The Highlanders will practice and play their games on the outfield of Humphries Diamond. Per league standards, the field of play can range between 50-80 yards in length and 30-50 yards in width, including a 10-yard end zone. “We’ll likely have over 20 games. There will be a league tournament at the end of the season.” Games are played in a 7-on-7 format with all seven players eligible as pass receivers, including the center after snapping the ball. There are no punts, field goals, or extra-point attempts—touchdowns are worth six points, while you can gain one extra point by converting a 5-yard play or twopoints from 10-yards. Punts automatically place the ball deep in the opponent’s half of the field. It’s a fast-paced game with two 22-minute halves, including a running clock for the first 20-minutes of each half. articles.text: Show continues in Mill Valley through May 28 Marin Theatre Company in Mill Valley currently is performing the West Coast premiere of Where Did We Sit on the Bus? Written by playwright Brian Quijada, with compositions by Satya Chávez, it will be performed now through Sunday, May 28. The play is a high-octane, tour-de-force theatrical experience that examines what it means to be of Latin heritage in America. The story begins in a third grade classroom, where students are learning about the civil rights movement and Rosa Parks. A young Hispanic girl raises her hand to ask her teacher, legacy and importance of Latin and Hispanic people and culture in the United States, through the inquisitive eyes of a young girl. Where Did We Sit on the Bus? Is a solo exploration infused with Latin rhythms, hip-hop, and live-looping, following that young student into adulthood as she navigates her own history and lineage. Directed by Matt Dickson and performed by Satya Chávez, the play will be performed on stage tomorrow, May 25, and Thursday, May 26. Closing night is Sunday, May 28. Visit https://www.marintheatre.org/productions/where-didwe-sit-on-the-bus to purchase tickets. articles.text: I acknowledge that in my travels I had never heard of the French writer, Sidonie-Gabrielle Colette, famous to millions as Colette, and best known in America for her novella Gigi, brought to the screen as a musical by Lerner and Loewe. She grew up in Burgundy in a middle-class home, surrounded by a bucolic beauty. Her life (1873-1954) was fulsome, encompassing three marriages, a daughter, numerous affairs, as well as living in Paris during the German occupation. The film Colette, while a biopic, is not hagiographic; rather it is a quietly engaging character study of a woman (Keira Knightly doing some of her best work) who lived a very individual life, often libertine in her choices. During her youth she married Henry Gauthier-Villars, a prolific writer using the nom de plume of Willy, some 15 years her senior. They lived in Paris where she reluctantly began to write a scandalous series titled Claudine, each semi-autobiographical, and all published as the work of Willy. The novels proved to be a sensation in Paris. As shown in one scene in the film, Willy, desperate for cash (he spends freely on women and the race track), locks Colette in a room, refusing to let her out until she writes the beginning chapters of another Claudine. If there is tension in the film – if tension is the right word – it Dominic West and Keira Knightley in Colette is how Colette attempts to detach herself from a marriage steeped in inequity. Willy is unrepentantly egotistical. However, it is clear that their relationship is, well, complicated, often driven by frustration, sparked by mutual infidelity as well as dependency, and cushioned by an affection that began as love. Colette also discovers that she is bisexual and at one point she and Willy share an American debutante staying in Paris. Meanwhile, Colette bridles at the fact that her prose, which has only improved, yet continues to be ghostwritten while Willy receives the fraudulent credits and accolades. Finally, Willy crosses a line that allows Colette to sever their marriage and she then enters into a relationship with a cross-dressing woman named Missy (Denise Gough) with whom she travels and performs as part of a theater group. It’s at this point that the film takes on a somber, more deliberate tone. Obviously, Colette is but one act in a life that was lived absent any strict adherence to even French norms. To say that she was unconventional does not begin to capture her willingness to risk all for what she desired as well as her art. Colette. Directed by Wash Westmoreland. articles.text: And so, finally, the popular culture juggernaut known as Harry Potter – meaning the gripping, stand in front of a bookstore at midnight to get the next book because this adventure is just too good – is coming to a close. The penultimate film, Deathly Hallows: Part I, has arrived. It amounts to a long setup, preparing the legions of serious fans for the grand finale that will follow.. Beginning in 1998 with Harry Potter and the Sorcerer’s Stone, the books and the films have all defied expectations. Start with the idea that young readers would lug home the equivalent of a phone book, eagerly squirrel themselves away in their rooms and read, and read nonstop. And with each movie, wait in long lines, impatient to see Harry (Daniel Radcliffe), Hermione Granger (Emma Watson) and Ron Wesley (Rupert Grint) survive their days at Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry. Legions of young and old readers have all taken the journey with Harry as he has morphed from a young orphan at Hogwarts, filled with uncertainty, into a young man who, along with his friends, now stands alone against his nemesis, the epitome of evil, Lord Voldemort (Ralph Fiennes). If you’re not a Potterhead then this movie will be a complete mystery. Not a thing will make sense. But then, these films are not made for walk-in-cold audiences who wouldn’t know a wizard from a Muggle. What is indisputable is that it’s beautifully shot, made possible by state-ofthe-art CGI, and filled with firstrate performances by endlessly talented English actors. For the fans who are completely plugged-in, then all is wonderfully clear. A footnote: that this story, when taken as a whole, sprang from the imagination of R.K. Rowling represents a stunning achievement in storytelling and is truly remarkable. Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows: Part I. Starring Daniel Radcliffe, Rupert Grint, Emma Watson. Directed by Daniel Yates. 2 hrs., 26 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2010. Now Streaming on Prime/VUDU/ Apple tv. articles.text: Nathan Gamble and Winter the Dolphin in a scene from Dolphin Tale If there are kids somewhere in the house, don’t hesitate to make the case that Dolphin Tale is sweet and moving and worth seeing. The youngsters will relish every minute. The film is based on the true story of Winter, a young dolphin that became entangled in a crab fisherman’s lines and was washed up on the Gulf Coast, near Clearwater, Florida. Seriously injured, she is nursed back to health by the staff at the Clearwater Marine Aquarium (CMA). And so the story begins. Sawyer Nelson (Nathan Gamble), 11-years-old, lonely, who was abandoned by his father some years before, his grades suffering, is resisting spending the summer enrolled in summer school. And it’s on the way to school early one morning, he discovers the bleeding dolphin on the beach and helps the fisherman cut her loose from the entangling net. And it’s then, in that moment, he and the dolphin make a connection, one that will change his life forever. Unbeknownst to his mother, Lorraine (Ashley Judd), he begins visiting the CMA every day (skipping school) and soon discovers a world where people are dedicated to rescuing and caring for marine mammals so they can eventually be released back into the environment. The refuge is run by Dr. Clay Haskett (Harry Connick, Jr.) with the help of his daughter, Hazel (Cozi Zuehlsdorff), also a pre-teen like Sawyer, who gives the dolphin the name Winter. And It’s at the CMA that he soon meets young Hazel; Dr. Clay; and Reed Haskett (Kris Kirstofferson), Clay’s father. But most importantly, he deepens his bonds with Winter, who is now struggling to survive. With regret, Dr. Haskett makes the decision to surgically remove Winter’s tail in order to save her life, and then sets about trying to create a prosthetic tail with the help of Dr. Cameron McCarthy (Morgan Freeman) of the VA Hospital. If there is help for Winter he can find it. How Winter’s life is changed parallels the changes brought about in the life of Sawyer. All are transformed, and in some way rescued in a wonderful, uplifting way. Dophin Tale is a family movie not to be missed. Dolphin Tale. Directed by Charles Martin Smith. Starring Nathan Gamble, Harry Connick, Ashley Judd, Cozi Selldorf, Kris Kristofferson and Morgan Freeman. 1 hr., 53 min. Rated PG. Released in 2011. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv supported by a fine cast led by James Gandolfini as New York’s lame duck mayor and John Turturro in the role of a NYC hostage negotiator. The Taking of Pelham 123 is filmed on the streets of New York, in the subway tunnels beneath the city, and within the confines of the Lexington Line car, offering stark contrasts between light and dark, all of which creates a powerful sense of foreboding. If you appreciate the genre, Pelham will be decidedly entertaining. The Taking of Pelham 123. Directed by Tony Scott. Starring Denzel Washington, John Travolta, John Turturo, Michael Rispoli and Luiz Guzman. 1 hr. 26 min. Rated R. Released in 2009. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/ Netflix.

articles.text: On Saturday, a mini music festival was held on the lawn in front of Studio One near Oakland Tech High School. There was music of all kinds, including small chamber ensembles, jazz, folk music and light rock. The only large ensemble was a combination of the Piedmont Chamber Orchestra, the Oakland Civic Orchestra, and some members of the former Holy Names Orchestra. articles.text: Dear Jim: I am about to start on a new retaining wall project in my backyard. I’ve received several bids, but they vary dramatically. I’m not sure I need a permit, and the unlicensed landscaper that was recommended to me is about half the price of the licensed contractors. Would it be OK to go for the unlicensed bid if they do good work? –Harry S. It’s Complicated There are a variety of factors to consider when picking the right person or company to do your project, whether they are licensed or not. Some of these are obvious, but there may be other issues to consider that are more subtle, which I will try to briefly outline here. Licenses and Permitting Most jobs require building or trade permits, with some notable exceptions. Different cities or jurisdictions have slightly different rules regarding what projects are permittable or that might require planning and zoning approval that will determine the size or where on the property things can be built. Piedmont tends to be more restrictive, but in many communities work like driveways, walkways, landscape retaining walls (less that 3’), fences 6’ or less, and a variety of interior work such as cabinets, flooring, painting, and wallpapering, etc. are not regulated. Once you check on your specific project with the city, if no permits are required then you are clear to work with an unlicensed vendor if you choose to. Liability and Risk Unlicensed folks are generally uninsured, which makes you liable for any injuries that might occur on the job, damage to your property, improper work, or their failure to complete the project or return afterwards should any issues arise. Since unlicensed workers are often less financially solvent than licensed contractors, they are less likely to stick around should problems arise and may not come back to correct them. Limited knowledge base; scope of work Even if your unlicensed company has good intentions, the fact that their jobs are done without approved plans, design or engineering, or inspections means that it may be difficult to monitor the progress and quality of the work. When jobs are more complex there are more likely to be issues. For example, fence building may be basic, but the details of designing and installing a proper drainage system or the dimensions and rebar placement in a concrete wall, etc. may require knowledge they don’t possess or drawings that aren’t available. These can be critical details that determine if the work stands the test of time. The Bottom Line If the job is simple enough and doesn’t required permits, do your homework. If you have someone unlicensed you want to hire, make sure your homeowner’s insurance covers the project or upgrade it for the work. Check their references and previous projects. Further, have them sketch out what they plan on doing and fact check it with someone licensed or do some online research to validate their approach. Finally, when in doubt, get somebody licensed (preferably with 20-30 years doing your specific type of work) and you will sleep better knowing your bases are covered. articles.text: Linh Becker, Jane Hammond and Boxcar Flower Farm Longtime friends and tennis partners Linh Becker of Piedmont and Jane Hammond of Berkeley created Boxcar Flower Farm as a pandemic-era passion project. Since taking over the farm in spring 2020, however, business has bloomed beyond all expectations. Jess Myles, the florist from whom the pair purchased the farm, had owned Boxcar since 2016, running many youth farming apprenticeship programs at the historic 16th Street Train Station in West Oakland. “When Jess had to leave for family matters on the East Coast,” said Becker, “we knew it would be an ideal project. As a result, we had a fantastically happy and healthy [time during the] pandemic, being able to bring flowers to our community outdoors.” Hammond met Becker as members of the same team at the Berkeley Tennis Club about seven years ago. “Although we both knew a fair amount about gardening, over the past three years, it’s been a steep learning curve figuring out what grows best and when,” said Hammond. The soil and setting of Boxcar, located in the former parking lot of the landmark station — which has not serviced trains for 30 years — proved perfect for the farm. The land is less than a quarter of an acre, and Becker and Hammond make use of every inch. Since 2020, they have acquired a fertilizer bin with over 100,000 worms, a beehive, a rain collection system, a farm cat, and countless monarch and swallowtail butterflies to pollinate the blooms. Currently, the farm is financially sustained by its Community Supported Agriculture (CSA) shares. On specified days, Berkeley-based subscribers pick up flowers from the farm or from Hammond’s house. On other days, Piedmont- and Oakland-based subscribers pick up flowers from the farm or from Becker’s house. Hammond estimates that 50-60% of Boxcar’s subscribers (now numbering more than 60) have been with the farm since the beginning. The pair has also gained a devoted following at Thornhill Coffee House in Montclair, where Boxcar bouquets are sold. “We’ve grown so much, we donate flowers to just about anybody who asks,” said Becker. articles.text: Photo courtesy of Oakland Zoo Donna, a 44-year-old elephant at Oakland Zoo since 1989, will be moved to a sanctuary in Tennessee next month. Oakland Zoo announced that it is moving Donna – a 44-yearold, 9,000-pound elephant who has resided at the zoo since 1989 – to a large sanctuary in Tennessee in early June. One of the last African elephants remaining in a Bay Area zoo, Donna bonded for life with Lisa, a 46-year-old elephant. In the wake of Lisa’s death last month, zookeepers felt that Donna would remain healthier among other female African elephants who bond with each other even more closely than with males. Colleen Kinzley, the zoo’s Vice President of Animal Care, said that for over three decades, Donna and Lisa would spend every night sleeping next to each other and almost all of their time in close proximity. “In the week or so following Lisa’s death,” she added, “we definitely noticed a big difference in Donna. She was unsettled, she was calling, vocalizing for Lisa … not having those female relationships is leaving a very big hole in her social opportunity and her overall quality of life.” Since the Oakland Zoo does not breed elephants, it must receive them from other zoos if it is to sustain its population. However, cohabitation with other species, like Indian elephants, was not advisable due to varied habitat, health, and size requirements. After a yearlong nationwide search with the Association of Zoos and Aquariums (AZA), no compatible female African elephants in protected care were available to join Donna. Thus, the zoo decided to move her to the Elephant Sanctuary, a 3,000- acre refuge 85 miles southwest of Nashville. pages.text: 24 Wednesday, May 24, 2023 Chocolate Pudding - Oaxacan Style Photo by Deborah Quok Chocolate Pudding, Oaxacan Style is this week’s recipe. By Deborah Quok INGREDIENTS Here’s something that’s perfect for this weekend – but this recipe comes with a warning: May become habit forming! The original is Susana Trilling’s, and is one of her signature recipes, showcasing Oaxaca, Mexico’s famous product – Chocolate. Rich and chocolate-y, with hints of cinnamon, this dessert is creamy but with texture from bread and cherries. Use this recipe as a base to try variations of chocolates, breads, liqueurs, dried fruits and flavorings. A few advance tips: Made of cacao, sugar and cinnamon, Mexican chocolate is essential for authentic Mexican flavor. As with the chocolate, Mexican vanilla has a unique flavor profile. Use it for authenticity. Budin de Chocolate Oaxaqueño – Adapted from Susana Trilling, Seasons of My Heart Makes six, 6-ounce ramekins For the pudding: • 1/4 cup dried cherries • 2 tablespoons Cointreau liqueur • 1-3/4 cup sweet baguette, cut into 1/2-inch cubes • 8 ounces Oaxacan chocolate, such as Seasons of My Heart (substitute a Mexican chocolate such as Rancho Gordo’s) • 1/4 cup brewed coffee, strong • 1/8 teaspoon sea salt • 2 large eggs • 1/2 cup crème fraiche • 1/4 cup heavy whipping cream • 1/8 cup granulated sugar • 1/2 teaspoon Mexican vanilla • 1/8 teaspoon Mexican cinnamon For the topping: • 1 cup heavy whipping cream • 1/2 teaspoon Mexican vanilla • 1 ounce Oaxacan chocolate, grated GOOD THROUGH JUNE 2023 GOOD THROUGH JUNE 2023 PREPARATION Preheat oven to 350˚F. Put the dried cherries and Cointreau in a small saucepan and bring to a simmer. Remove from heat and let cherries continue to soak. Spread bread cubes on a baking sheet and bake until lightly toasted, 10-15 minutes. Set aside. Put the chocolate, coffee and salt into a double boiler over barely simmering water. Stir occasionally while the chocolate melts. Whisk until smooth. Allow to cool. Put the eggs, crème fraiche, cream, sugar, vanilla and cinnamon in a medium sized bowl and whisk until blended. Add the melted chocolate and continue stirring until thoroughly blended. Add the soaked cherries, with any remaining liqueur, and toasted bread cubes; stir well. Set aside at room temperature until the bread completely soaks up the mixture, about 2 hours. (This can be made a day ahead; refrigerate the mixture.) When ready to bake, preheat the oven to 350˚F. Bring a kettle of water to a boil. Divide the pudding mixture into six buttered ramekins. Put them in a baking pan large enough to hold them all without touching. Slide out the oven rack, put the pan on the rack; then pour in the boiling water to come halfway up the sides of the ramekins. Avoid getting water into the puddings. Bake until the puddings are set but still moist, 45-50 minutes. Check to see if done by inserting a clean knife into the center of a pudding. If it comes out clean, the pudding is ready. Remove from the oven and place on a rack to cool. After 15 minutes, remove the puddings from the ramekins, if desired. For the topping: whip the cream and vanilla together to desired consistency. Serve puddings with plenty of whipped cream and grated chocolate. articles.text: The city has already begun implementing some of the programs. These include an incentive passed by the City Council late last November to make it easier for Piedmonters to convert existing spaces into ADU housing. The city also issued a Request for Proposals on January 23 to seek a consultant for the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan. A major part of the Element, this plan would include 132 new units of housing on 18 acres of city-owned land on both sides of Moraga Canyon, to include Blair Park. Consequences for Piedmont Piedmont is subject to the “Builder’s Remedy,” a clause added to California’s Housing Accountability Act in 1990 by which developers can file an application for a housing development which does not comply with a city’s local zoning laws. Any development applied for under the Builder’s Remedy must have 20% of its units available to lower-income households, or all its units available to middle-income households or transitional or supportive housing. However, state restrictions still hold — significantly the California Environmental Quality Act, a statute passed in 1970 by then-governor Ronald Reagan which limits proposed building projects on the grounds of potentially “significant environmental effects.” Planning & Building Director Kevin Jackson has said that the Builder’s Remedy is “generally a tool used by developers in cities where there are available sites or “where somebody has been working on a project for a while and now have their opportunity to push it forward. It’s not really that useful for properties that have no developer interests, because it takes time to figure out what kind of project makes sense.” Under the Remedy, any noncompliant city is also ineligible for state grants and funding for road repair and infrastructure. However, Jackson confirmed that city staff has been “researching the grants we do get and expect to get,” and there are none for which this late adoption period renders Piedmont ineligible. More information about the Housing Element and IS-ND is available at PiedmontisHome.org. For questions about the Element, contact Kevin Jackson by email at kjackson@piedmont.ca.gov.

According to Palmer, work is scheduled to begin on June 6 and should be completed by December 1. Earlier renovations of the field involved converting the grass field to FieldTurf, an artificial grass, to eliminate the field flooding every winter. Most contracts with the FieldTurf company specified that the warranty for the life of its product was approximately eight years. The current field surface was last replaced in 2007, 16 years ago. The renovation is expected to include: • Perforated subsurface drainage; surface perimeter trench drains; a drain mat; perm drain rock; drainage at the top of the bleachers; additional area drains • Storm drain rerouted from its current location under the field, to follow the Wildwood side of the track through to the Bushy Dell Creek manhole • Restored existing track • Erosion control for construction • Removal of existing turf; new synthetic turf and recyclable infill • Hardscape demolition, base material excavation • ADA-compliant concrete paving and ramps on the west side of the Field House • Seismic foundations for football, softball and hardball fields • Goal posts and lacrosse nets • New scoreboards Schedule, impacts Palmer told the Post that the “heavy lifting” of the project will be “in June, August and September.” There will be an estimated eight days of truck activity in June (when turf will be hauled out), “not a lot” in July (when drainage systems including underground piping will be installed), nine in August (when drain rock will be installed), and ten in September. Palmer told the approximately 30 participants at the meeting that, over the course of the project, 400 truckloads would be brought back and forth along Palm Drive. The primary entrance and exit route for trucks navigating Palm will be along Winsor Avenue. Contractor vehicles will also use El Cerrito Avenue and park in the Witter Field parking lot. The path to the dog park will be sectioned off, said Palmer, “along with the bleachers, the track and the synthetic turf field. You’ll still be able to get to the hardball field by walking on the El Cerrito side.” “No parking” signs will be in place on Palm Drive and parts of Wildwood, Park View, and Winsor Avenues through September. Occasional “no parking” restrictions will be in place on El Cerrito and Jerome Avenues near Witter Field. Per the presentation, construction schedule assumes a No Parking start time of 7 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. “When school starts up in August, we could actually get the trucks in there and out before student drop-off,” Palmer said. Palm Drive resident Anastasia Edel, who attended the meeting with her husband, Misha, said “Given that more water will go through an old pipe rerouted into a storm drain, many neighbors are concerned of new flood risks to their basements.” “When we asked why Palm Drive was chosen as the truck route and what the city’s plan was for dealing with noise and safety measures for neighborhood kids or damage to the street after such heavy use,” she added, “we were shut down again: ‘The engineers did their studies, I won’t discuss it here.’” Fliers announcing the Monday night meeting were distributed to affected households on Thursday, May 18, four days in advance. The meeting itself was two weeks prior to the planned start of construction on June 6. Some households received no fliers at all. “Palmer made it sound like a done deal. The discussion wasn’t about why they were using our tax money to do such a drastic project in such an aggressive, last-minute manner, it was people confused about what impacts they would face in the first place. He was repeating ‘We want the voices of our community to be heard,’ but it was so perfunctory,” Misha said. “Evidently they did all of this prior planning, but we were notified only two weeks before the project was supposed to begin. They did such a poor job of explaining the details,” he added. “Coordination between the city and the school wasn’t what it should have been. Given the relatively unpleasant summer we, the neighbors, all expect as a result, the question now is: ‘How can the school cooperate with the city to make neighborhood voices heard going forward?’” Project background Construction to renovate Witter Field’s turf and irrigation system was approved by the Piedmont School Board on January 25. The price tag for this effort to avoid flooding of the community’s principal sports field was $4,156,933, and a contract in that amount was awarded to Robert Bothman Construction. However, Palmer told the Post, “All in all, we’re expecting it to be right around $5 million. We’re hoping we can raise some funds to pay for things like the scoreboards, which are about $360,200 [and] $270,000.” Bothman was also the low bidder in 2019 with a bid of $3.5 million. Under former School Superintendent Randy Booker, the project stalled and work was never begun. The school district plans to use State Modernization Funds to pay for the project. This funding is tied to the H1 bond, which paid for the new Alan Harvey Theater and the STEAM building. The district’s General Fund will not be used for the project. The current turf of the field is well beyond its eight-year life span. In 2007, when it was installed and still under warranty, the new turf cost $219,000, with installation in two weeks. Similar to the many years when the field was grass, the field has flooded and been unplayable for periods of time each winter due to rain and insufficient drainage. For questions contact Facilities Director Pete Palmer at 594- 2877 or by email at ppalmer@ piedmont.k12.ca.us. Witter Field flooded significantly in 2017, following a six-year drought. articles.text: IS YOUR HOUSE IN A LIVING TRUST? Many of us postpone putting our houses in a trust because a) we are busy, b) we do not like to think about death and dying, and c) we do not fully understand the consequences of not having our assets in a living trust. California is a probate state. The probate process is lengthy, expensive, and complex; especially if there are disputes among beneficiaries. By placing our homes in a trust, we can control the distribution of funds from our estate, and ensure that our estate does not unnecessarily spend money on attorneys, court fees, appraisal fees, and other professional fees which can greatly reduce the estate’s overall value. If an estate goes through probate, here is the schedule of attorney fees for “ordinary services:” 1. Four percent on the first $100,000 2. Three percent on the next $100,000 3. Two percent on the next $800,000 4. One percent on the next $9,000,000 5. One-half of one percent on the next $15,000,000 6. Above $25,000,000, a reasonable amount will determined by the court (Source: Probate Code, https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/) We calculated the base amount an estate would likely pay in probate attorney fees if we had a $1,000,000 estate and a $5,000,000 estate: • $1,000,000 estate would pay $23,000 • $5,000,000 estate would pay $63,000 Yet, the cost to the estate goes well beyond the basic probate attorney fees. The cost also includes months of lost time dealing with the probate court system, appraisals, and professional service fees that may be required. Further, an estate may be assigned a real estate agent who is more inclined to turn properties quickly than ensure that heirs receive the maximum sales price. This could lead to a loss of hundreds of thousands of dollars for the estate. The cost of putting property and assets into a revocable trust typically runs $2,000 - $4,000. The process often takes 2 - 4 weeks and includes 2 - 3 attorney meetings. “Death is the ultimate surprise, but it shouldn’t be a surprise that it’s a surprise.” ADDITIONAL TRUST BENEFITS Tax Benefits There may be ways to reduce estate taxes and gift taxes to help minimize the capital gains taxes on property sales. Protection from Creditors A trust may be able to help shield assets from potential lawsuits or other legal actions. Privacy Avoiding Conservatorship Placing a house and assets in a trust can help to keep financial affairs private and out of the public record. With a properly structured trust, a trust-designated trustee can manage assets rather than a court-appointed conservator. Faster Asset Distribution Assets in a trust can typically be distributed to beneficiaries much more quickly than assets that go through probate. Flexibility Trusts offer flexibility in terms of how assets are managed and distributed. Trusts can be updated as needed as long as the trustee is mentally competent. Protection for Blended Families For families with children from previous marriages, a trust can help ensure that assets are distributed amongst beneficiaries as desired. Avoiding Ancillary Probate Ancillary probate is required when the estate owns property in a state other than the state of residence, and can be costly and time-consuming. By placing out-of-state property in a trust, ancillary probate can be avoided. “The importance of holding assets, including real property, in a trust, is significant,” says Kenneth Hecht, an attorney with Knox Ricksen, LLP. “In addition to the savings in avoiding the time, expense, and inconvenience of probate proceedings, a revocable estate planning trust allows the trustee to manage, and if needed, sell the trust assets both during the lives of, and upon the death of, the creators (or Grantors) without court involvement.” SALES IN APRIL BY CITY April 2022 vs April 2023 Dedicated to clients, culture, and community, Calia Homes is a team of exceptional real estate professionals who work together with the common goal of providing unparalleled client services in a supportive and collaborative environment.
